title: Card Rewards & Traps
description: Rewards, teaser rates, and the fees that eat them.
wolfLine: A reward you pay interest to earn is not a reward.

cash-back.definition: A card reward that returns a percentage of what you spend, as money.
cash-back.example: 2% cash back on $1,000 of spending is $20.

intro-apr.definition: A temporary low rate, often 0%, that lasts for a set number of months and then jumps to the regular APR.
intro-apr.example: 0% for 12 months, then 24%. The debt still left in month 13 is charged 24%.

balance-transfer.definition: Moving debt from one card to another, usually to a lower rate. The new card often charges a fee of a few percent.
balance-transfer.example: Transfer $2,000 with a 3% fee and you owe $2,060 on the new card.

lessons.title: Cash-Back Math
lessons.summary: A percent of what you spend. It never covers interest you did not have to pay.

steps.context: [[Cash back]] returns a slice of your spending. 2% of $100 is $2. It is real money only if you were going to spend that $100 anyway.
steps.prompt: A card pays 2% cash back. You spend $2,500. How much do you get back?
You spend $800 at 1.5% cash back. How much is the reward?
The same month you pay $40 of interest. What is the reward minus the interest?
steps.explain: $12 − $40 = −$28. The “reward” month cost you $28.

steps.prompt: When is cash back actually a gain?
choices: When you pay the statement in full, so you are not buying the reward with interest
When you carry a balance
When you spend more just to earn it
steps.explain: Interest eats rewards fast.

steps.prompt: Earning 2% back means the purchase was 2% cheaper, even if you pay interest on it.
steps.explain: Interest can cost more than the reward.

steps.prompt: You do not need the item. It offers 5% back. What do you do?
choices: Skip it. A reward on a wasted purchase is still wasted money
Buy it for the 5%
Buy two
steps.explain: Five percent back on $100 you did not need is $5, and you are out $95.

lessons.title: Points or Cash
lessons.summary: Turn the points into cents before you call them generous.

steps.context: Points are just cash back in costume. Divide the reward by the points to get a value in cents. If 100 points equal $1, each point is worth one cent, which is 1% back.
steps.prompt: A program says 1 point per dollar, and 100 points equal $1. What is a point worth?
choices: 1 cent
1 dollar
steps.explain: 100 points = $1, so 1 point = 1 cent.

steps.prompt: You earn 2,000 points at 1 cent each. What are they worth in dollars?
A 2% cash-back card on the same $2,000 of spending pays how much?
How much more does the 2% card pay than those 2,000 points?
A bonus category pays 3 points per dollar, still at 1 cent a point, at grocery stores. What is that in percent?
steps.explain: 3 cents per dollar is 3%.

steps.prompt: A point is always worth more than a cent of cash back.
steps.explain: Check the redemption. Some points are worth less than a cent.

lessons.title: Rewards That Cost More
lessons.summary: If you spend extra to chase the bonus, you lost.

steps.context: A reward you would not have earned on a purchase you would not have made is not a discount. It is a reason someone hoped you would spend.
steps.prompt: A jacket is $100. You do not need it, but the card pays 5% back. How much is the reward?
After the $5 reward, how much did the unneeded jacket really cost you?
You carry the $100 for a year at 24% APR. Rough interest?
steps.explain: $100 × 0.24 = $24, against a $5 reward.

steps.prompt: Interest $24, reward $5. How much are you behind?
steps.explain: $24 − $5 = $19 behind, plus you own a jacket you did not need.

steps.prompt: A sign that says “5% back” means you should buy something.
steps.explain: It means the price is 5% less only if you were buying it anyway, and only if you pay in full.

steps.prompt: Which spending earns a reward that is really yours?
choices: The grocery run you were making anyway, paid in full
A gadget you bought for the points
A balance you are paying interest on
steps.explain: Planned spending, no interest.

lessons.title: Is the Annual Fee Worth It?
lessons.summary: The extra percent has to earn the fee before you are ahead.

steps.context: Subtract the annual fee from the rewards. If you will not spend enough for the extra percent to cover the fee, the free card wins.
steps.prompt: The bonus card pays 2 percentage points more (3% instead of 1%). The fee is $80. How much must you spend before that extra 2% covers the fee?

steps.prompt: On $4,000 of spending, what does the 1% card pay?

lines.label: Cash back on $4,000 of spending at 1%

steps.prompt: On $4,000, what does the 3% card pay after its $80 fee?
You only spend $2,000. The 3% card pays $60 before the fee. What is left after the $80 fee?
steps.explain: $60 − $80 = −$20. You paid for the privilege.

steps.prompt: You spend about $2,000 a year on the card and always pay in full. Which card?
choices: The 1% card with no fee
The 3% card with the $80 fee
They come out the same over a year
steps.explain: At $2,000 the fee eats the bonus and more.

steps.prompt: A higher cash-back rate is a better deal even when you barely use the card.
steps.explain: The fee can be bigger than the rewards.

lessons.title: The 0% Intro Rate
lessons.summary: Zero has an expiration date. The balance that remains does not.

steps.context: An [[intro APR]] is a teaser, often 0% for 12 or 15 months. When it ends, the regular [[APR]] applies to whatever [[balance]] is left. Miss a payment and some offers end early.
steps.prompt: What is an intro APR?
choices: A temporary low rate that ends on a set date
A rate that stays 0% for as long as you own the card
A fee
steps.explain: Read the number of months. That is the whole sale.

steps.prompt: You move $1,800 onto a 0% intro rate for 15 months and pay $120 a month. How much have you paid after 15 months?
Is anything left to charge the regular rate on?
steps.explain: $1,800 − $1,800 = $0. You finished inside the window.

steps.prompt: Suppose you pay only $60 a month for those 15 months. How much is left when the 0% ends?
steps.explain: $60 × 15 = $900 paid. $1,800 − $900 = $900 still owed, now at the regular APR.

steps.prompt: A 0% intro rate means the purchase is free.
steps.explain: It means interest is postponed. The principal is still due.

steps.prompt: You cannot pay the balance off before the intro rate ends. What should you assume?
choices: The leftover balance will cost the regular APR
The 0% will renew itself
The bank will forgive the rest
steps.explain: Plan for the rate on the letter, not the rate in the ad.

lessons.title: Balance Transfers
lessons.summary: Read the offer: a lower rate can be worth a fee, if the debt gets paid.

steps.context: A [[balance transfer]] moves debt to a new card. The fee, often 3%, is added to what you owe. A 0% window only helps if you pay the debt down before it shuts.

lessons.title: Store Cards
lessons.summary: Today’s discount can cost more than it saves.

steps.context: Store cards often pair a same-day discount with a very high [[APR]]. The discount is yours only if you were buying the item, and only if you do not carry the balance.
steps.prompt: A $150 jacket is 20% off if you open the store card. How much is the discount?
What is the sale price?
You carry that $120 for a year at 30% APR. Roughly how much interest?
How much more is the interest than the discount you “saved”?
steps.explain: $36 − $30 = $6. You paid for the sale.

steps.prompt: You can pay the $120 today in cash. Should you open the store card for the discount?
choices: No. Pay cash. The card’s rate is the trap, and you do not need it
Yes. Store cards always help a credit score
Yes, and leave the balance for a year
steps.explain: A discount you can already afford in cash does not require a 30% card.

steps.prompt: A store card at a high APR is a cheap way to build credit if you carry a balance.
steps.explain: On-time and paid in full builds credit. Carrying a 30% balance just costs money.

lessons.title: Jay’s Rewards Chase
lessons.summary: He earned $30 and spent $400 he did not need to spend.

story.title: The rewards chase
story.body:
Jay’s card pays **5%** back at restaurants this quarter. He starts eating out so the category “pays him.” In three months he puts **$600** on the card. About **$200** of that was meals he would have bought anyway.

He pays the statement in full, which is the one part he gets right. The extra **$400** was spent to chase the bonus.

steps.prompt: How much cash back does Jay earn on the $600?
How much of the $600 was extra spending he would not have done?
steps.explain: The story: $600 − $200 of ordinary meals = $400.

steps.prompt: After the $30 reward, how much did that extra spending cost him?
What went well?
choices: He paid the statement in full, so he did not add interest
The extra meals were free
5% back means he made money overall
steps.explain: No interest. The waste was the extra $400.

steps.prompt: Spending more in a bonus category is a good idea whenever the percent is high.
steps.explain: The percent applies to money leaving your account.

steps.prompt: What should Jay do next quarter?
choices: Use the 5% on meals he was buying anyway, and skip the rest
Double his restaurant budget
Open three more cards for the same chase
steps.explain: Rewards ride along. They do not pick the purchase.
